links.outcome: Self-reported decision switching after AI heatmap and binary feedback among expert radiographers
links.effect: Only two of 216 responses (1.1%) indicated they would change their mind; 15.7% might; 83.5% would retain initial decision. No significant correlation between trust and decision switching.
links.quote: Of the total 216 responses to this question across all datasets there were only two instances (examination 11b and 1c) where participants indicated that they would change their mind in response to the AI feedback (1.1%), n = 35 (15.7%) indicated that they might change their mind from their initial diagnosis and the remainder (n = 179, 83.5%) indicated that they would retain their initial decision.

links.outcome: Clinician agreement with GradCAM heatmap localisation as a measure of explanation clinical meaningfulness
links.effect: Radiographers disagreed with heatmaps in 45.8% (n=66) of pathological images; perfect agreement 22.2% (n=32); partial 31.9%. Agreement with heatmap correlated with trust (tau -.515).
links.quote: There was perfect agreement with the heatmap noted in 22.2% of images (n = 32), partial agreement in 31.9% of images (n = 46) and disagreement in 45.8% of images (n = 66).

links.effect: Discordant AI binary feedback included three false positives and one false negative.
links.quote: Of those where the consensus diagnosis of the participants differed from the AI binary feedback, three were false positive, where the AI determined pathology in examinations where the radiographer did not and one false negative, where the AI failed to detect a pathology identified by the participant ( Fig 6 ).
